eyebrow: KEY STAGE 3 HISTORY • YEAR 7 ENQUIRY CHRONOLOGY • 15 MILESTONES

eras.title: Part 1: Luther, Henry VIII & The Break with Rome (1517–1547)
Part 2: Elizabeth I’s Middle Way & The Spanish Armada (1558–1588)
Part 3: Stuart Divine Right, Regicide & Parliamentary Supremacy (1603–1689)

milestones.title: Martin Luther’s 95 Theses & Spark of the Reformation
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Henry VIII break with Rome and destroy the monasteries?
milestones.imageCaption: Lucas Cranach the Elder, Portrait of Martin Luther (1529, Uffizi Gallery): German monk whose 1517 protest against papal indulgences ignited the European Reformation.
milestones.catalyst: Across early sixteenth-century Europe, anger grew at Catholic officials selling **indulgences**—certificates claiming money could buy forgiveness and shorten time in **Purgatory**.
milestones.turningPoint: In **October 1517**, German monk **Martin Luther** nailed **95 arguments** to the Wittenberg church door, using the printing press to challenge papal authority across Europe.
milestones.impact: Protestant ideas spread rapidly, though young **King Henry VIII** initially defended Catholic sacraments and won Pope Leo X’s proud title **Defender of the Faith**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Within ten years, Henry’s desperate need for a male Tudor heir turned Rome’s champion into the Pope’s fiercest royal rival.

keyTerms.definition: A 16th-century religious movement that challenged papal Catholic authority and created Protestant churches.
A certificate sold by Catholic officials promising forgiveness of sins and reduced time in Purgatory.

milestones.title: Henry VIII’s Dynastic Crisis & The Roman Deadlock
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Henry VIII break with Rome and destroy the monasteries?
milestones.imageCaption: Cardinal Thomas Wolsey (National Trust): Henry VIII’s chief minister who fell from power in 1529 after Pope Clement VII revoked the Blackfriars annulment trial.
milestones.catalyst: Fearing civil war because Queen **Catherine of Aragon** had borne no surviving son, **Henry VIII** fell in love with **Anne Boleyn** and demanded a papal **annulment**.
milestones.turningPoint: Because Catherine’s nephew **Emperor Charles V** sacked Rome in May 1527 and held **Pope Clement VII** prisoner, the Pope cancelled Cardinal Wolsey’s London trial in 1529.
milestones.impact: Wolsey was stripped of office and arrested, convincing Henry that no foreign Pope should hold legal power over the English Crown.
milestones.bridgeToNext: To bypass Rome legally, sharp-minded lawyer Thomas Cromwell turned to England’s Reformation Parliament.

keyTerms.definition: Relating to a hereditary line of rulers from the same family and the struggle to secure their unbroken succession.
A legal or religious declaration that a marriage was invalid from the beginning and never truly existed.

milestones.title: Thomas Cromwell & The Reformation Parliament’s Break with Rome
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Henry VIII break with Rome and destroy the monasteries?
milestones.imageCaption: Hans Holbein the Younger, Portrait of Thomas Cromwell (1532–1533, Frick Collection): Chief minister who drafted the parliamentary statutes severing England from papal rule.
milestones.catalyst: Blocked by papal diplomacy, chief minister **Thomas Cromwell** realised Henry could sever Rome’s authority using binding **statute laws** voted by MPs.
milestones.turningPoint: Between 1529 and 1533, the **Reformation Parliament** halted church tax payments to Rome and passed the **1533 Act in Restraint of Appeals**, banning legal appeals to the Pope.
milestones.impact: Archbishop Cranmer annulled Henry’s first marriage and crowned **Anne Boleyn**, unintentionally elevating **King-in-Parliament** as England’s supreme law-making partnership.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Having broken Rome’s legal grip, Henry and Cromwell moved in 1534 to seize direct leadership and wealth of the English Church.

keyTerms.definition: A formal written law passed by Parliament and approved by the monarch, possessing supreme legal power.
Supreme, independent power and legal authority over a state, free from any external control or foreign ruler.

milestones.title: The 1534 Act of Supremacy & Dissolution of 800 Monasteries
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Henry VIII break with Rome and destroy the monasteries?
milestones.imageCaption: Ruins of Fountains Abbey, North Yorkshire: Dissolved in 1539 when Henry VIII and Thomas Cromwell closed over 800 monasteries and sold their estates.
milestones.catalyst: To cement total religious control and replenish the royal treasury, Henry demanded sworn loyalty oaths and ordered Cromwell to survey Church wealth.
milestones.turningPoint: Parliament’s **1534 Act of Supremacy** named Henry **Supreme Head of the Church of England**; dissenters like **Sir Thomas More** were executed, and over **800 monasteries** were dissolved (1536–1540).
milestones.impact: Selling monastic estates enriched the Crown and gave landowning gentry a lasting financial stake in keeping England Protestant in Parliament.
milestones.bridgeToNext: After fierce Protestant shifts under Edward VI and nearly 300 Marian Catholic burnings, Elizabeth I inherited a fractured kingdom in 1558.

keyTerms.definition: The state of holding ultimate, unquestioned legal and religious authority within a kingdom.
The official dismantling, closure, and confiscation of Catholic monasteries and abbeys by Henry VIII.

milestones.title: Elizabeth I’s 1559 Religious Settlement & The Via Media
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Elizabeth I try to settle England’s religious divisions after 1558?
milestones.imageCaption: Title page of Queen Elizabeth I’s 1559 Book of Common Prayer (British Library), establishing one English prayer book across every parish.
milestones.catalyst: Inheriting England in **1558** after Mary I burned nearly **300 Protestant martyrs** while returning **Puritans** demanded strict reform, **Elizabeth I** needed peace to avoid civil war.
milestones.turningPoint: Parliament’s **1559 Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity** styled Elizabeth **Supreme Governor** and introduced one English **Book of Common Prayer** backed by **12-pence** recusancy fines.
milestones.impact: Elizabeth’s **Via Media** (‘Middle Way’) secured broad outward conformity across parishes without making ‘windows into men’s souls’.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Peace did not last: the arrival of Catholic claimant Mary, Queen of Scots in 1568 soon sparked rebellion and papal fury.

keyTerms.definition: The compromise legal title chosen by Elizabeth I in 1559 to appease Catholics and Puritans.
Latin for "The Middle Way": Elizabeth I’s strategic policy of balancing Protestant and Catholic practices.
A person (almost always Catholic) who refused to attend compulsory Church of England services on Sundays.

milestones.title: Revolt of the Northern Earls & Pope Pius V’s Excommunication
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Elizabeth I try to settle England’s religious divisions after 1558?
milestones.imageCaption: Bartolomeo Passarotti, Portrait of Pope Pius V (Walters Art Museum): Issued the 1570 papal bull Regnans in Excelsis excommunicating Elizabeth I.
milestones.catalyst: Traditionalist Catholic **Northern Earls** rebelled in **1569**, storming Durham Cathedral to smash Protestant communion tables and celebrate Latin Mass.
milestones.turningPoint: After Elizabeth crushed the revolt and executed **400 rebels**, **Pope Pius V** issued the **February 1570 papal bull *Regnans in Excelsis*** excommunicating Elizabeth as a heretic.
milestones.impact: By releasing English Catholics from their oath of allegiance, the Pope turned every practising Catholic into a suspected traitor in the eyes of Parliament.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Encouraged by Rome’s decree, underground conspirators plotted to assassinate Elizabeth and crown Mary, Queen of Scots.

keyTerms.definition: An official decree by the Pope expelling someone from the Catholic Church and declaring them damned.
A formal proclamation, letter, or charter issued by the Pope, bearing an authentic lead seal (bulla).

milestones.title: Walsingham’s Spies, The Babington Plot & Execution of Mary Stuart
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did Elizabeth I try to settle England’s religious divisions after 1558?
milestones.imageCaption: Contemporary engraving of the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots in the Great Hall of Fotheringhay Castle on 8 February 1587.
milestones.catalyst: Imprisoned in England, **Mary, Queen of Scots** became the focal point for Catholic plots, culminating in **Anthony Babington’s 1586 conspiracy** to murder Elizabeth.
milestones.turningPoint: Protestant spymaster **Sir Francis Walsingham** intercepted coded letters smuggled inside **beer barrels**, proving Mary’s treason and leading to her execution at **Fotheringhay** on **8 February 1587**.
milestones.impact: Beheading an anointed Catholic queen removed Elizabeth’s domestic rival, but handed **King Philip II of Spain** papal backing to invade England.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Before Philip II’s invasion fleet could sail from Spain, Sir Francis Drake launched a daring pre-emptive strike on Cadiz.

keyTerms.definition: The practice of spying or using secret agents to uncover government treason and foreign plots.
A secret code or mathematical system of writing used to disguise the meaning of conspiratorial letters.

milestones.title: Singeing the King of Spain’s Beard: Drake’s Raid on Cadiz
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Philip II’s Spanish Armada fail to invade England in 1588?
milestones.imageCaption: Sir Francis Drake’s April 1587 raid on Cadiz harbour, destroying Spanish warships and burning seasoned oak barrel staves.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Voyage & Wrecks of the 1588 Spanish Armada from Spain through the English Channel and around Scotland and Ireland.
milestones.catalyst: Angered by English aid to Dutch Protestant rebels, Drake’s Caribbean raids, and Mary Stuart’s execution, **King Philip II** assembled a vast Catholic **Armada**.
milestones.turningPoint: In **April 1587**, **Sir Francis Drake** sailed straight into **Cadiz harbour**, destroying **30 Spanish vessels** and burning warehouses of seasoned oak barrel staves.
milestones.impact: Drake’s raid delayed the Armada by a full year and forced Spain to store water and food in green-wood casks that rotted at sea.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Even with rotting supplies, 130 Spanish ships entered the English Channel in July 1588 in a tight crescent formation.

keyTerms.definition: An armed, privately owned warship commissioned by a government to raid enemy merchant shipping.
The detailed coordination and management of complex military operations, supplies, and food at sea.

milestones.title: Calais Fireships, Gravelines & Defeat of the Spanish Armada
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Philip II’s Spanish Armada fail to invade England in 1588?
milestones.imageCaption: English fireships packed with pitch and gunpowder drift toward the anchored Spanish Armada off Calais at midnight on 7–8 August 1588 (National Maritime Museum).
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Midnight fireships at Calais, the Battle of Gravelines, and Atlantic shipwrecks off Scotland and Ireland (August–September 1588).
milestones.catalyst: Shadowed up the Channel by nimble English **race-built galleons**, the **130-ship Armada** anchored off **Calais** on 7 August 1588 awaiting the Duke of Parma’s army.
milestones.turningPoint: At midnight, English captains sent **eight blazing fireships** into the anchorage; panicked Spanish ships cut their cables, lost formation, and were battered by **culverin broadsides** at **Gravelines**.
milestones.impact: Fierce **‘Protestant Wind’** gales wrecked dozens of ships off Scotland and Ireland; only **67 vessels** returned, cementing England’s Protestant patriotic identity.
milestones.bridgeToNext: When Elizabeth died childless in 1603, the new Stuart kings shattered Tudor cooperation with Parliament by claiming absolute Divine Right.

keyTerms.definition: A wooden ship packed with gunpowder, pitch, and tar, set ablaze and steered into anchored enemy fleets.
The simultaneous firing of all artillery guns mounted along one side of a warship.
The protective care and direct intervention of God in human affairs and historical battles.

milestones.title: Stuart Accession & The Doctrine of Divine Right of Kings
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Which turning point shifted power most decisively from monarchs to Parliament?
milestones.imageCaption: John de Critz the Elder, King James I of England and VI of Scotland (c. 1606): First Stuart monarch of England, who asserted the Divine Right of Kings before Parliament.
milestones.catalyst: While Tudor monarchs had governed in partnership with MPs through statute law, the Stuart dynasty inherited the English throne under **James I** in **1603**.
milestones.turningPoint: **James I** and his son **Charles I** championed the **Divine Right of Kings**, insisting monarchs were God’s lieutenants on earth and stood above parliamentary criticism.
milestones.impact: Repeated clashes over royal finances, foreign war, and religion poisoned trust at Westminster and led Charles I to dismiss MPs completely in **1629**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Ruling alone without MPs for eleven years, Charles I stretched ancient royal taxes across inland England.
keyAgents: King James I & King Charles I

keyTerms.definition: A political system in which a monarch holds total, unrestricted power over government and subjects.
Written laws formally passed by Parliament and approved by the monarch, superior to royal decrees.

milestones.title: The Eleven Years’ Tyranny & John Hampden’s Ship Money Stand
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did conflict with Parliament cost King Charles I his head—and reshape monarchy?
milestones.imageCaption: John Hampden (c. 1595–1643): Buckinghamshire MP whose 1637 refusal to pay inland Ship Money rallied resistance against Charles I’s Personal Rule.
milestones.catalyst: Dismissing MPs in **1629**, **Charles I** governed alone during the **Eleven Years’ Personal Rule**, while **Archbishop William Laud** enforced ceremonial Church reforms that angered Puritans.
milestones.turningPoint: To raise money without parliamentary votes, Charles extended coastal **Ship Money** to inland counties; in **1637**, landowner **John Hampden** refused to pay, sparking nationwide tax boycotts.
milestones.impact: When Scottish rebels resisted Laud’s prayer book and bankrupted the Crown, Charles was forced to recall a furious Parliament in **1640**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Returning MPs attacked royal courts and ministers until Charles marched armed guards into the Commons chamber.
keyAgents: King James I & King Charles I

keyTerms.definition: The period from 1629 to 1640 when King Charles I ruled England without summoning Parliament (the Eleven Years’ Tyranny).
An ancient coastal tax that Charles I illegally extended to inland counties without parliamentary consent to raise royal funds.

milestones.title: Attempted Arrest of the Five MPs & Outbreak of Civil War
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did conflict with Parliament cost King Charles I his head—and reshape monarchy?
milestones.imageCaption: John Singleton Copley, Charles I Demanding the Surrender of the Five Impeached Members in the House of Commons (4 January 1642).
milestones.catalyst: Recalled in 1640, Parliament abolished royal prerogative courts, impeached the King’s ministers, and demanded control over ministers and militias.
milestones.turningPoint: On **4 January 1642**, **Charles I** marched armed guards into the **House of Commons** to arrest **Five MPs** for treason, only to find the warned MPs had escaped by river into London.
milestones.impact: Humiliated by his failed coup, Charles fled the capital and raised his royal war flag at **Nottingham in August 1642**, plunging England into civil war.
milestones.bridgeToNext: After three years of inconclusive regional fighting, Parliament forged Britain’s first professional national army in 1645.
keyAgents: King James I & King Charles I

keyTerms.definition: A formal charge of treason or high crimes brought by Parliament against a royal official or minister.
The belief that a monarch’s authority comes directly from God and that no earthly court or parliament can judge them.

milestones.title: The New Model Army & Decisive Victory at Naseby
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did conflict with Parliament cost King Charles I his head—and reshape monarchy?
milestones.imageCaption: The Battle of Naseby, 14 June 1645 (National Army Museum): Sir Thomas Fairfax and Oliver Cromwell’s New Model Army routs King Charles I’s Royalist forces.
milestones.catalyst: Early Royalist successes exposed the weakness of local militias, prompting Parliament in **1645** to form the professional, merit-promoted **New Model Army**.
milestones.turningPoint: Commanded by **Sir Thomas Fairfax** and **Oliver Cromwell**, disciplined redcoat cavalry smashed Charles I’s flanks at the **Battle of Naseby** on **14 June 1645**.
milestones.impact: Parliament captured Royalist artillery and Charles’s secret letters seeking foreign troops, destroying the King’s military hopes.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Refusing to accept defeat, Charles secretly sparked a Second Civil War—convincing Army leaders the ‘man of blood’ had to stand trial.
keyAgents: Oliver Cromwell & The New Model Army
King James I & King Charles I

keyTerms.definition: Oliver Cromwell’s professional, disciplined Parliamentary force, promoted on military ability rather than aristocratic birth.
The crime of betraying the sovereign state or attempting to overthrow its lawful government and constitution.

milestones.title: Pride’s Purge, Regicide of Charles I & The Commonwealth
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did conflict with Parliament cost King Charles I his head—and reshape monarchy?
milestones.imageCaption: The Trial of King Charles I in Westminster Hall, January 1649 (Library of Congress): An anointed English monarch tried for high treason against his own people.
milestones.catalyst: Outraged after Charles plotted a second civil war with Scottish allies, **Colonel Pride’s troops** purged moderate MPs from Westminster in December 1648, leaving the radical **Rump Parliament**.
milestones.turningPoint: Tried before a High Court of Justice for treason against his people, **King Charles I** was publicly beheaded outside **Whitehall** on **30 January 1649**.
milestones.impact: Parliament abolished the monarchy and House of Lords to declare a republican **Commonwealth**, proving an anointed king was subject to the law.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Although the monarchy returned in 1660, fears of Catholic absolutism under James II triggered one final revolution in 1688–1689.
keyAgents: Oliver Cromwell & The New Model Army
King James I & King Charles I

keyTerms.definition: The deliberate public trial and execution of a reigning monarch (such as King Charles I in January 1649).
The republican government of England, Scotland, and Ireland established after the execution of Charles I (1649–1660).

milestones.title: The Glorious Revolution, Bill of Rights & Parliamentary Supremacy
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Which turning point shifted power most decisively from monarchs to Parliament?
milestones.imageCaption: Romeyn de Hooghe, Joint Coronation of King William III and Queen Mary II, April 1689 (Rijksmuseum): Crowned under the binding conditions of the 1689 Bill of Rights.
milestones.catalyst: After the **1660 Restoration**, Catholic **King James II** alarmed Protestant nobles, who invited Dutch Prince **William of Orange** to land at Torbay in November 1688 as James fled to France.
milestones.turningPoint: In the **Glorious Revolution**, Parliament crowned **William III and Mary II** only after binding them to the **December 1689 Bill of Rights**.
milestones.impact: Kings could never again suspend laws, levy taxes, or keep a peacetime army without MPs’ consent, permanently enthroning **constitutional monarchy** and Parliamentary supremacy.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Lasting Legacy: Across 1517–1689, supreme power in Britain shifted permanently from Rome and absolute monarchs to elected MPs in Parliament.
keyAgents: William III & Mary II (1689 Bill of Rights)

keyTerms.definition: The landmark 1689 law establishing that the Crown cannot suspend laws, levy taxes, or maintain an army without Parliament.
A system of governance in which a monarch shares power with an elected parliament and rules strictly under the law.
